newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Rebels control at least one-sixth of Zaire.
newsitem.headline: Rebels control at least one-sixth of Zaire.

text.p: Rebels advancing on the northeastern capital of Kisangani have seized at least one-sixth of Zaire, Africa's third largest country, since the start of the revolt last October.

They control a stretch of eastern Zaire bordering on Sudan, Uganda, Rwanda, Burundi and Tanzania which is more than 1,000 km (600 miles) long from north to south and in places 300 km (190 miles) wide.

It is by far the largest single area held by rebels opposed to President Mobutu Sese Seko since he seized power in a coup in 1965. Mobutu has survived several insurgencies, but the foreign help he received in the past has not been forthcoming this time.
Analysts of the conflict said that probably more than five million people out of Zaire's total population of about 44 million now live under rebel rule.
Rebel strategy has focused on hitting cities and towns in the east with airports vital to a government counter-offensive ordered by leaders in Kinshasa, in the extreme west of Zaire.
In their most recent triumphs, rebels say they overran the town of Kindu on the Zaire river with a large air base and Lubutu, the last major town on the road from Bukavu in the east to Kisangani.
Rebel leader Laurent Kabila says the rebels' main target is Kisangani, Zaire's third largest city downriver from Kindu with its own airbase and the main centre for any counter-offensive.

The rebels control about a half of Haut Zaire, at 500,000 square km the largest of the eight regions in the country, most of Kivu province to the south and in the southeast perhaps five percent of mineral-rich Shaba, Zaire's second largest region.
Kivu is the most populous region in Zaire with more than five million people but only the fifth largest in terms of area.

The main overall direction of the rebel offensive since October has been counter-clockwise north from the city of Bukavu bordering on Rwanda to Goma and then on to Bunia before turning westwards to Isiro and then swinging southwest towards Kisangani.
This thrust took them from the mountains around Bukavu to the coffee and tea-growing high savannah of the northeast before descending into a dense jungle plateau stretching across Zaire's interior.
At the same time rebels pressed south from Bukavu to Uvira and then to the port of Kalemie, Kabila's birthplace, on Lake Tanganyika and west and northwest towards Kindu and Kisangani.

The rebel advance has also secured control over many mining areas including gold and diamond centres but the rebels still have to make major inroads into copper-rich Shaba towards Lubumbashi, Zaire's second largest city and its mining capital.
